explanation: Start with the widest pair. Move the shorter boundary inward: keeping it while reducing the width cannot improve the area, so only replacing that boundary can lead to a better container.
timeComplexity: O(n) Each step moves a boundary inward, for at most n−1 steps.
spaceComplexity: O(1) Two pointers and the best area are the only working state.
attribution: Unmodified EPIJudge reference source: epi_judge_java_solutions/epi/MaxTrappedWater.java. Original contributors; repository LICENSE: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/).
correctness: The current shorter boundary limits the pair’s water height. Any narrower pair retaining that boundary cannot have a greater area, so discarding that boundary loses no improving answer. Repeating this elimination considers an optimal pair before either of its necessary boundaries can be safely discarded.
walkthrough: For heights [2,1,5,3], the widest pair uses indices 0 and 3, width 3 and height 2, giving area 6. The remaining pairs are narrower and produce no area above 6.
edgeCases: Fewer than two boundaries gives area zero.
Width is the distance between indices.
This container problem differs from summing rainwater above every bar.
